topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.title: Proof of Irrationality
topic.student_journey: Understand → See → Try → Think → Build → Solve → Apply → Master → Retain
topic.syllabus_scope_note: Comprehensive proofs of irrationality for √2, √3, √5, √7 and algebraic extensions to linear combinations such as 3 + 2√5, 5 - √3, and 1/√2.

current_focus: Proof of irrationality of √2, √3, √5 using Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (Theorem 1.2)
Proof by contradiction using coprime representation p/q with gcd(p,q)=1
Divisibility corollary: If prime p divides a², then p divides a
Proofs for linear combinations and surds: a + b√c, a - √b, 1/√a, a√b
excluded_from_this_topic: Euclid division lemma (deleted from current CBSE syllabus)

learning_objectives: Define rational numbers (p/q, q ≠ 0, p,q ∈ Z) and irrational numbers.
Understand the structure of Proof by Contradiction (Reductio ad Absurdum).
Represent assumed rational numbers in lowest terms with gcd(p,q)=1.
Apply Theorem 1.2: If a prime p divides a², then p divides a.
Construct complete algebraic contradiction proofs for √2, √3, and √5.
Rearrange and isolate surds in linear expressions (e.g. 3 + 2√5) to deduce contradiction.
Identify and correct common logical fallacies in irrationality proofs.

learning_sequence.title: 1. Rational vs Irrational Numbers
learning_sequence.summary: Every real number is either rational or irrational.

points.text: Rational Number: Can be written as p/q where p, q are integers, q ≠ 0, and gcd(p,q) = 1 (lowest terms).
Irrational Number: Cannot be written as a fraction. Its decimal is non-terminating and non-recurring (e.g. √2, √3, π).

learning_sequence.title: 2. The Strategy: Proof by Contradiction
learning_sequence.summary: Prove a statement by demonstrating that its opposite is impossible (Reductio ad Absurdum).

points.text: Conclusion: Our premise was false, so √2 MUST be irrational.

learning_sequence.title: 3. The Crucial Coprime Condition
learning_sequence.summary: The contradiction hinges entirely on the lowest-terms assumption.

points.text: Assume √2 = p/q with gcd(p, q) = 1 (no common factor other than 1).
If later steps force both p and q to share a common factor (like 2), this directly shatters the coprime premise.

learning_sequence.title: 4. Theorem 1.2: Prime Divisibility Corollary
learning_sequence.summary: Let p be a prime number. If p divides a², then p divides a.

points.text: Reason: By FTA, a = p₁p₂...pₖ. Then a² = p₁²p₂²...pₖ².
Since p is prime and divides a², uniqueness of FTA forces p to be one of the prime factors of a.

learning_sequence.formula: p is prime and p | a² ⇒ p | a

steps.text: Contradiction: 2 divides both p and q, violating gcd(p,q) = 1! Hence √2 is irrational.

learning_sequence.title: 6. Linear Combinations & Surd Forms (a + b√c)
learning_sequence.summary: For linear forms like 3 + 2√5, isolate the radical on LHS:

steps.text: Contradiction: RHS is Rational (integers closed under +, -, ×, ÷), but LHS (√5) is Irrational. Rational ≠ Irrational!

learning_sequence.title: 7. ⚠️ Critical Board Exam Traps
learning_sequence.summary: Watch out for these common marking deductions in CBSE exams:

points.text: Theorem 1.2 ONLY applies to PRIMES! Composite Counterexample: 4 divides 6² (36), but 4 does NOT divide 6 (because 4 is composite).
Missing Coprimality: Forgetting to write 'where p and q are coprime integers and q ≠ 0' loses 1 full mark.

learning_sequence.trap: Always specify that p and q are coprime (gcd(p,q)=1) and q ≠ 0!

mnemonics.text: Basic Root Proof: Assume Rational → Coprime p/q → Square p² = 2q² → Prime Divides p (p=2k) → Substitute (q²=2k²) → Prime Divides q → Contradict gcd(p,q)=1 → Conclude
Linear Surd Form (a + b√c): Assume a/b → Isolate √c on LHS → RHS is Rational (Integers closed under +,-,×,÷) → LHS is Irrational → Contradiction!

worked_examples.title: See How the Proof Is Built

steps.reason: Assume on the contrary that √2 is rational. Let √2 = p/q where p, q are integers, q ≠ 0, and gcd(p,q) = 1 (lowest terms).
Square both sides to eliminate the radical: (√2)² = (p/q)² ⇒ 2 = p²/q² ⇒ p² = 2q².
2 divides 2q², so 2 divides p². Since 2 is prime, by Theorem 1.2, 2 divides p. Thus p = 2k for some integer k.
Substitute p = 2k into p² = 2q²: (2k)² = 2q² ⇒ 4k² = 2q² ⇒ q² = 2k². Since 2 is prime and divides 2k², 2 divides q² ⇒ 2 divides q.
2 divides both p and q, meaning p and q have a common factor 2. This contradicts our assumption that gcd(p,q)=1. Hence, √2 is irrational.
Assume on the contrary that √3 is rational: Let √3 = p/q where p, q ∈ Z, q ≠ 0, and gcd(p,q) = 1.
Square both sides: 3 = p²/q² ⇒ p² = 3q².
3 divides 3q², so 3 divides p². Since 3 is prime, by Theorem 1.2, 3 divides p. So let p = 3k for integer k.
Substitute p = 3k into p² = 3q²: (3k)² = 3q² ⇒ 9k² = 3q² ⇒ q² = 3k². Since 3 is prime and divides 3k², 3 divides q² ⇒ 3 divides q.
3 is a common factor of both p and q, contradicting gcd(p,q)=1. Hence our assumption is false and √3 is irrational.
Assume on the contrary that √5 is rational: Let √5 = a/b where a, b are integers, b ≠ 0, and gcd(a,b) = 1.
Square both sides: 5 = a²/b² ⇒ a² = 5b².
5 divides 5b², so 5 divides a². Since 5 is prime, by Theorem 1.2, 5 divides a. So let a = 5k for some integer k.
Substitute a = 5k into a² = 5b²: (5k)² = 5b² ⇒ 25k² = 5b² ⇒ b² = 5k². Since 5 is prime and divides 5k², 5 divides b² ⇒ 5 divides b.
5 divides both a and b, meaning a and b have a common factor 5. This contradicts gcd(a,b)=1. Hence, √5 is irrational.

examples.question: Prove that 1/√2 is irrational, given that √2 is irrational.

steps.reason: Let 1/√2 = a/b where a, b ∈ Z and a, b ≠ 0.
Taking reciprocals isolates √2.
Since a and b are integers with a ≠ 0, b/a is rational. This implies √2 is rational, which contradicts the fact that √2 is irrational.
Therefore, 1/√2 is irrational.
